lesson.label: 📖 Bài học chính
lesson.title: 1. Coffee Shops vs. WFH
lesson.context: ***Context:*** *Ryan and Emma are friends who both work remotely. Emma meets Ryan for lunch at a coffee shop.*
lines: Emma
Hi! Have you been here all morning?
Ryan
Since nine. I work here most days now. I find it hard to focus at home, so I like to **get out of the house**.
Emma
Really? I can’t do that. I find coffee shops a bit **distracting:** the music, people chatting, someone on a phone call…
Ryan
I see your point, but for me, a bit of **background noise** actually helps. At home, it’s too quiet, and I **end up** lying on the sofa, **scrolling through** my phone.
Emma
I’ve set up **a proper workspace** at home: a desk, a good chair and a second screen. Once I sit down there, I’m **in work mode**. For me, it’s **a matter of discipline**.
Ryan
That’s great if you have the space. My flat’s tiny, and my bed is right next to my desk. It’s **way too tempting**.
Emma
**Fair enough.** Doesn’t it get expensive? A drink every day really **adds up**.
Ryan
Yeah, it’s not cheap. But if I **get more done** in three hours here than in a whole day at home, it’s **worth it**.
Emma
What about the Wi-Fi? Last time I worked in a café, it kept **cutting out** during a video call.
Ryan
That does happen. That’s why I always have **a back-up plan**. I use my phone as **a hotspot**.
Emma
And are you comfortable taking calls **in public**?
Ryan
Not really. If I have an important meeting, I stay home. So I suppose **it depends on** what kind of work I’m doing.
Emma
That makes sense. Maybe I’ll **give it a try** for simple tasks, like answering emails.
Ryan
Come with me tomorrow. **Worst case**, you get a good coffee.

lesson.title: 2. Hustle Culture
lesson.context: ***Context:*** *Anna and Josh are friends. They’re meeting for dinner on Friday evening, and Anna has just arrived, an hour late.*
lines: Anna
Sorry I’m late. I had to finish a report, and then my manager asked for one more thing.
Josh
**No worries.** Is it always like this at your new job?
Anna
**Pretty much.** Most people in my team stay until eight or nine. If you leave at six, it looks like you’re not **committed**.
Josh
Even if you’ve finished your work?
Anna

Yeah, it’s just the culture there. And to be honest, I don’t mind that much. I’m still **early in my career**, so I want to **prove myself**. If I **put in the hours** now, I’ll **get promoted** faster.
Josh
I get that. But I’m not sure **working longer** always **means working better**. Some of my colleagues stay late, but they spend half the evening chatting or on their phones.
Anna
That’s true for some people. But **in my industry**, everyone works long hours. If I don’t, someone else will **take my place**.
Josh
Maybe. But you’ve **cancelled on** us three times this month. Do you ever get time to **switch off**?
Anna
Not really. Even at the weekend, I check my emails. I **feel guilty** if I don’t reply **straight away**.
Josh
That’s what worries me. My last job was like that, and after a year, I was completely **burnt out**. I couldn’t sleep, and I **lost interest in** everything.
Anna
I didn’t know that. What happened after that?
Josh
I moved to a company with more **reasonable hours**. I leave at six, I **turn off notifications** at the weekend, and honestly, my work is better because I’m not exhausted all the time.
Anna
I guess **there’s a difference between** working hard **and** working all the time.
Josh
Yeah. I’m not saying you shouldn’t be **ambitious**. I just think you need to **set some boundaries**.
Anna
Maybe I could start by not checking emails on Sundays.
Josh
That sounds like **a good start**. Now, let’s order. I’m **starving**.

homework.title: Part 1: Vocab check
homework.instructions: Fill in each blank with a phrase from the word bank. Use each phrase once.
homework.context: Hannah and Leo work at the same marketing agency. Their company has just announced a trial of a four-day working week.
lines: Hannah
Have you heard? We’re trying a four-day week from January.
Leo
I know. Honestly, I’m a bit worried. If we only work four days, won’t clients think we’re less {committed}?
Hannah
I don’t think so. Our clients care about results, not how many hours we {put in}.
Leo
Maybe. But we’re already really busy. Won’t we just {end up} working late every Thursday?
Hannah
I see your point, but some studies show that people actually {get more done} in four days, because they waste less time.
Leo
{Fair enough}. But I check my emails at the weekend anyway. I’m not sure an extra day off will help me {switch off}.
Hannah
That’s {a matter of discipline}, though. You could just turn off your notifications.
Leo
Easier said than done. When I don’t reply straight away, I {feel guilty}.
Hannah
I get that, but if you never rest, you’ll be completely {burnt out} by the summer.
Leo
True. I suppose {it depends on} the kind of work we do. Let’s just see how the trial goes.
Hannah
Exactly. And if it doesn’t work, we can always go back.

homework.title: Part 2: Listening
homework.intro: Listen to part of a podcast about a rule one manager tried at work, then do Parts A and B.
homework.podcast: 🎧 Work Talk: the phone box experiment

script.text: Welcome back to Work Talk. Today, I want to share a small experiment we tried at my company. It caused more arguments than I expected.

Last spring, I noticed that in almost every meeting, ==half the team were looking at their phones==. Some were checking emails, and some were obviously on social media. So I made a rule: no phones in meetings. Everyone had to leave them in ==a box by the door==.

For the first two weeks, I thought it was a great success. ==Meetings were shorter, and people actually listened to each other.== But then the complaints started. One colleague, Sara, pointed out that she sometimes needed her phone to check information during meetings, ==because her laptop was too slow==. Another colleague had a young ==child== and was worried about missing a call from the school.

Honestly, my first reaction was to say no. ==I thought they were just making excuses.== But when I thought about it more, I realised they had a fair point. The problem wasn't really the phones. ==The problem was that people were bored, and some of our meetings were simply too long.==
So we changed the rule. ==Now, phones can stay on the table, but face down, and we keep every meeting under thirty minutes.== If someone needs to take an urgent call, they just ==step outside==.

Has it worked? Mostly, yes. People still check their phones sometimes, but much less than before. And I've learned something about debates at work: if you really listen to the other side, you usually end up with a better solution than the one you started with.
